Exact moments of order statistics with orderStatMoments

Source: vignettes/orderStatMoments.Rmd
orderStatMoments.Rmd

What this package computes

Order statistics are the sorted values of a sample, X(1)≤…≤X(n)X_{(1)} \le \dots \le X_{(n)}. Many statistics are built from them, for example, a sample median or quantile, the range, a trimmed mean, the best linear unbiased estimators of location and scale, or a mean and a standard deviation imputed from a reported five-number summary. The mean and the standard error of such a statistic require the means, variances and covariances of the order statistics it uses. Without the exact values, one falls back on simulation or on large-sample approximations, whose error is largest at the extreme ranks and in small samples. The tables of the covariances of normal order statistics printed in the literature stop at n=50n = 50. The software we found gives the means, or the means and variances, of single order statistics, or approximates the covariances.

The orderStatMoments package computes these moments exactly, for any ranks and any sample size, by numerical integration of their defining integrals, or by closed-form expressions where the distribution has them. Thirteen families are built in and are given as in R, by name and with R’s own parameters: the normal, uniform, exponential, logistic, Gumbel, Student tt, Cauchy, gamma, chi-square, beta, lognormal, Weibull and FF distributions. Any other continuous distribution enters through its distribution, density and quantile functions. Building on the moments, three more functions are provided. os_quantile_weights() gives the weights of a sample quantile under any of the nine definitions of R’s quantile(). os_lin_moments() gives the means and covariances of any linear combinations of order statistics. os_blue() gives the best linear unbiased estimators (BLUE) of location and scale of Lloyd (1952).

The package has two requirements. The distribution must be continuous, and a moment is computed only if it exists, which the package checks rank by rank from the tail behavior of the distribution (set by the package for a built-in family, and declared in the tail argument of os_dist() for a user’s distribution). Here “exact” means the finite-sample integral evaluated numerically, as opposed to a large-sample or series approximation. The integrator is asked for a relative tolerance of 10−1110^{-11} on a single integral and 10−910^{-9} on the outer integral of a covariance. A tolerance is the accuracy asked of the integrator. It is not a bound on the error of the result (see “What the result holds”).

The package’s tests, which R CMD check runs, compare the quadrature with values known from other sources: closed forms, printed tables and exact identities. All the tolerances below are absolute differences, unless they say otherwise. The tests check the quadrature against the closed forms of the uniform and the exponential at the five ranks of a five-number summary and all their pairs, for n=20n = 20, 100 and 1001, within 10−1010^{-10}. For the normal, they check the ten-decimal tables of Tietjen, Kahaner and Beckman (1976) within 10−710^{-7}, the accuracy those tables certify, on the entries printed correctly (Appendix B says which are not). They also check the mean and variance of the range tabulated by Harter (1960), within 2×10−82 \times 10^{-8} up to n=97n = 97. On a complete set of ranks, the order statistics are a permutation of the sample, so their moments satisfy identities such as “the means sum to nn times the parent mean”. The tests assert these identities within 10−910^{-9}. The largest residual, the difference between the two sides of an identity, that we measured on the full matrices of the five families up to n=100n = 100 was 1.1×10−121.1 \times 10^{-12}. Wu and Tong (2026) describe the computation and these checks in full, and compare the package with other software.

The call is one function:

m <- os_moments(
  n = 20,                   # the sample size
  ranks = c(1, 5, 10, 20),  # the order statistics to compute (default: all)
  dist = "norm"             # the name of a built-in family, as in R,
                            # or a distribution built with os_dist()
)
m
#> Exact moments of order statistics: norm (mean = 0, sd = 1), n = 20, ranks 1 5 10 20
#> alpha (means):
#>          r1          r5         r10         r20 
#> -1.86747500 -0.74538300 -0.06199629  1.86747500 
#> B (covariance matrix):
#>             r1         r5        r10        r20
#> r1  0.27569660 0.05705664 0.02965625 0.01020472
#> r5  0.05705664 0.09399600 0.04933743 0.01707114
#> r10 0.02965625 0.04933743 0.07694744 0.02688388
#> r20 0.01020472 0.01707114 0.02688388 0.27569660
#> route: integrate; quadrature error estimate: 1.5e-11
#> checks: reflection n/a; identities n/a

The print shows the means of the four order statistics of a standard normal sample of 20 (alpha) and their covariance matrix (B), with the variances on its diagonal. “What the result holds” describes the other fields. The last line, checks, shows n/a here. The two run-time checks of Appendix B need all the ranks 1 to nn, or a rank set that contains n+1−rn + 1 - r whenever it contains rr, such as 1, 5, 16 and 20 at n=20n = 20.

Use the family name when the distribution is one of the thirteen, with its parameters under R’s own names (see “Installation and the families”). For another distribution, build it once with os_dist() (see “A user-supplied distribution”). For the means and the variances at many ranks without the covariances, pass cov = FALSE, which skips the double integrals. The help page ?os_moments lists every argument.

Computing cost

This section helps the user size a computation before asking for a full matrix. Each mean and each variance is one integral over the real line. Each covariance is a double integral, evaluated as nested quadrature, and costs far more. The chunk below prints the times, in milliseconds, on the machine that built this vignette.

t_single <- system.time(os_moments(100, ranks = c(1, 50, 100),
                                   cov = FALSE))[["elapsed"]]
t_pairs  <- system.time(os_moments(100, ranks = c(1, 50, 100)))[["elapsed"]]
t_full10 <- system.time(os_moments(10))[["elapsed"]]
t_full20 <- system.time(os_moments(20))[["elapsed"]]
round(1000 * c(three_means_and_variances = t_single,
               with_three_covariances = t_pairs,
               full_matrix_n10 = t_full10, full_matrix_n20 = t_full20))
#> three_means_and_variances    with_three_covariances           full_matrix_n10 
#>                         5                       443                      2272 
#>           full_matrix_n20 
#>                      9667

The computing cost of one integral hardly depends on nn. On an Apple M3 Pro, for the standard normal and nn from 5 to 1001, a single integral took 0.19 to 0.25 ms and a double integral 36 to 76 ms. A call at the five ranks of a five-number summary, with their ten covariances, took 0.6 to 0.8 seconds for the uniform and the exponential at n=104n = 10^4, 10510^5 and 10610^6. So a few ranks cost well under a second, whatever the sample size.

A full matrix is different. At sample size nn it needs n(n−1)/2n(n-1)/2 covariances, or about half as many for a symmetric family, so its time grows with the square of nn. By that count, the full matrix at n=100n = 100 costs about 26 times the one at n=20n = 20 above. On the machine that built this vignette, that predicts about 251 seconds. On the M3 Pro, the full normal matrix took 2.4 minutes at n=100n = 100 on one core, and 70 minutes at n=1001n = 1001 on 12 cores. For nn in the hundreds, run one call of os_moments() per pair of ranks in parallel, rather than one call for the whole matrix. The package has no helper for this. Each call returns the 2 by 2 covariance matrix of its pair.

Installation and the families

This section says how to install the package and how a built-in family is given. Install it from GitHub, with the vignette:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ZWuLab/orderStatMoments", build_vignettes = TRUE)

To cite the package in a publication, use citation("orderStatMoments"), which gives the paper of Wu and Tong (2026).

The package imports nothing beyond base R and stats. A built-in family is given as in R: dist is the name that R’s functions carry after p, d and q ("gamma" for pgamma()), and its parameters are passed by R’s own names, with R’s defaults. A user who can write rgamma(n, shape = 2, rate = 3) already knows the call. The families are the twelve continuous distributions for which base R provides the p, d and q functions, and the Gumbel, which R does not provide.

dist Parameters, with R’s defaults Closed forms returned by default
"norm" mean = 0, sd = 1 none; all moments by quadrature
"unif" min = 0, max = 1 every mean, variance and covariance
"exp" rate = 1 every mean, variance and covariance
"logis" location = 0, scale = 1 the means and the variances
"gumbel" location = 0, scale = 1 (maximum form, F(x)=exp⁡(−e−x)F(x) = \exp(-e^{-x}) at the defaults) the mean and variance of the maximum
"t" df none
"cauchy" location = 0, scale = 1 none
"gamma" shape, and rate = 1 or scale none
"chisq" df none
"beta" shape1, shape2 none
"lnorm" meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1 none
"weibull" shape, scale = 1 none
"f" df1, df2 none

A parameter without a default must be given, and the noncentral versions (R’s ncp) are not built in. Every argument of os_moments() after dist is given by its full name.

By default the package uses a closed form wherever the family has one. For 20 exponential waiting times with mean 2, the means of the minimum, the tenth order statistic and the maximum come from closed forms:

# the order statistics of 20 exponential waiting times with mean 2 (rate 1/2)
e <- os_moments(20, ranks = c(1, 10, 20), dist = "exp", rate = 1/2)
e$alpha
#>       r1      r10      r20 
#> 0.100000 1.337543 7.195479
e$route
#> [1] "closed"

route says where the numbers came from. "closed" means the closed forms, and "integrate" the quadrature. "mixed" means that the family has closed forms for some of the requested quantities and not for others. method = "integrate" forces the quadrature everywhere, which is how the package’s tests check the quadrature against the closed forms.

The parameters of a family, a shift and a multiplier

This section shows the parameters at work and the two arguments that apply to every distribution. The order statistics of ten gamma observations with shape 2 and rate 3, and of ten lognormal observations, are requested as the random numbers would be:

g <- os_moments(10, ranks = c(1, 5, 10), dist = "gamma", shape = 2, rate = 3)
g$alpha
#>        r1        r5       r10 
#> 0.1553405 0.5250292 1.5409857
os_moments(10, ranks = c(1, 5, 10), dist = "lnorm", meanlog = 1, sdlog = 0.5,
           cov = FALSE)$alpha
#>       r1       r5      r10 
#> 1.312638 2.605240 6.136485

The package computes the moments of the standard member of each family, the member with the shape parameters of the call and R’s defaults elsewhere, and applies the other parameters afterwards, exactly. The mean and the standard deviation of the normal, the ends of the uniform, the rate of the exponential, the rate or the scale of the gamma, the scale of the Weibull and exp⁡(meanlog)\exp(\mathrm{meanlog}) of the lognormal are a shift and a multiplier of the standard member. So a distribution with a large mean or a small rate loses no digits, and the user does not have to know which parameter does what.

Two arguments apply to every distribution. os_shift =a= a and os_multiplier =b>0= b > 0 give the moments of the order statistics of Y=a+bXY = a + bX, where XX has the distribution of the call: the means become a+bE[X(r)]a + b\,E[X_{(r)}] and the covariance matrix is multiplied by b2b^2. They serve where a distribution has no parameter of its own for a shift or a multiplier, such as a tt distribution with a location and a scale, a shifted exponential, or a three-parameter Weibull:

# five observations from 3 + 2 T, with T a t variable with 5 degrees of freedom
os_moments(5, dist = "t", df = 5, os_shift = 3, os_multiplier = 2, cov = FALSE)
#> Exact moments of order statistics: t (df = 5), os_shift = 3, os_multiplier = 2, n = 5, ranks 1 2 3 4 5
#> alpha (means):
#>         r1         r2         r3         r4         r5 
#> 0.09804974 1.88398700 3.00000000 4.11601300 5.90195000 
#> var (variances; cov = FALSE):
#>       r1       r2       r3       r4       r5 
#> 4.591509 1.708025 1.400664 1.708025 4.591509 
#> route: integrate; quadrature error estimate: 3.89e-12
#> checks: reflection 1.61e-17; identities sum_alpha 2.94e-17, sum_sq 8.88e-16

The package also sets the tail behavior of each family, which decides the moments that exist (“A user-supplied distribution” states the rule). The Cauchy distribution has no mean, but the median of five Cauchy observations has a variance. The ranks 1, 2, 4 and 5 have no second moment, and os_moments() stops at the first such rank:

os_moments(5, ranks = 3, dist = "cauchy")$var
#>       r3 
#> 1.221253
os_moments(5, dist = "cauchy")
#> Error:
#> ! os_moments(): the moment of order 2 of X_(1) does not exist: the lower tail index 1 times the rank 1 is not above 2

A gamma, a chi-square, a Weibull, a beta or an FF distribution with a shape below 1 has a density that is infinite at an endpoint of its support. The package integrates next to such an endpoint in a variable in which the integrand is bounded (Appendix A), so these families take the same call, including the extremes at the sample sizes tested (Appendix B):

# the minimum and the maximum of 1001 observations from the arcsine law, beta(1/2, 1/2)
os_moments(1001, ranks = c(1, 1001), dist = "beta", shape1 = 0.5, shape2 = 0.5,
           cov = FALSE)
#> Exact moments of order statistics: beta (shape1 = 0.5, shape2 = 0.5), n = 1001, ranks 1 1001
#> alpha (means):
#>           r1        r1001 
#> 4.910174e-06 9.999951e-01 
#> var (variances; cov = FALSE):
#>           r1        r1001 
#> 1.199694e-10 1.199694e-10 
#> route: integrate; quadrature error estimate: 7.14e-17
#> checks: reflection 8.88e-16; identities n/a

What the result holds

This section names the fields of the result that a user reads first, and says what the error estimate is and is not. os_moments() returns an object of class "orderStatMoments".

Field Content
alpha the means E[X(r)]E[X_{(r)}], named by rank
var the variances
B the covariance matrix, with the variances on its diagonal (NULL when cov = FALSE)
route "closed", "integrate" or "mixed"
quad_err the sum of the error estimates that integrate() reported for the single integrals and for the outer integrals of the covariances
standard a list with the alpha, var and B of the standard member of the family, which os_blue() reads
par, os_shift, os_multiplier the parameters of the built-in family (NULL for a user’s distribution) and the two constants of the call
checks the residuals of the run-time checks (Appendix B), NA where a check did not apply

quad_err is an estimate, not a bound, for two reasons. The inner integral of a covariance does not pass its error estimate to the outer one. And the error of a mean is not propagated into the variance that subtracts its square, or into the covariances that subtract its product with another mean. Treat quad_err as a diagnostic. No certified error bound is stored. The evidence of accuracy is the agreement with closed forms, printed tables and identities, summarized above and in Appendix B.

That evidence has a limit worth knowing. The covariances with closed forms belong to the uniform and the exponential, which are both bounded below, so they do not test a double integral over an unbounded lower tail. For the normal beyond n=50n = 50, where no printed table exists, the checks are the identities on complete rank sets, which test sums of moments rather than each moment.

A user-supplied distribution

This section shows how to supply a distribution that is not built in, and the five points that matter for such a distribution. os_dist() builds the object that dist accepts, from the three functions of a distribution in R’s convention, with the parameters fixed inside them. Here is a Pareto distribution with shape 3 on [1,∞)[1, \infty), whose survival function is x−3x^{-3}:

pareto <- function(shape) os_dist(
  p = function(q, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE) {
    ls <- -shape * log(pmax(q, 1))          # log S(x) = -shape * log(x)
    if (lower.tail) { if (log.p) log(-expm1(ls)) else -expm1(ls) }
    else if (log.p) ls else exp(ls)
  },
  d = function(x, log = FALSE) {
    ld <- ifelse(x >= 1, log(shape) - (shape + 1) * log(x), -Inf)
    if (log) ld else exp(ld)
  },
  q = function(p) (1 - p)^(-1 / shape),
  support = c(1, Inf),      # the endpoints of the support
  tail = c(Inf, shape),     # bounded below; the density decays like x^(-shape-1) above
  name = "pareto"
)
os_moments(5, dist = pareto(3))
#> Exact moments of order statistics: pareto, n = 5, ranks 1 2 3 4 5
#> alpha (means):
#>       r1       r2       r3       r4       r5 
#> 1.071429 1.168831 1.314935 1.577922 2.366883 
#> B (covariance matrix):
#>             r1          r2          r3          r4         r5
#> r1 0.005886970 0.006422149 0.007224918 0.008669902 0.01300485
#> r2 0.006422149 0.018449080 0.020755220 0.024906260 0.03735939
#> r3 0.007224918 0.020755220 0.051165560 0.061398670 0.09209800
#> r4 0.008669902 0.024906260 0.061398670 0.180491600 0.27073740
#> r5 0.013004850 0.037359390 0.092098000 0.270737400 2.40885300
#> route: integrate; quadrature error estimate: 9.63e-12
#> checks: reflection n/a; identities sum_alpha 4.44e-16, sum_sq 7.11e-15, sum_B 4.69e-11

Every variance exists here, because νU(n−r+1)>2\nu_U (n - r + 1) > 2 at every rank when νU=3\nu_U = 3. The checks line gives the residuals of the three permutation identities of Appendix B. The reflection check does not apply, because the distribution is not symmetric.

  1. p must honor log.p and lower.tail, and d must honor log. The package evaluates the integrands on the log scale in both tails, through p(x, log.p = TRUE) and p(x, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE). The log scale keeps powers like F(x)r−1F(x)^{r-1} from underflowing to zero at large nn. A p that ignores these arguments, or that computes log(p(x)) from a probability that has already underflowed, loses the tails. The example forms log⁡S(x)\log S(x) directly and log⁡F(x)\log F(x) through expm1(). os_dist() checks that the arguments are honored at the median and the lower quartile, and that d integrates to one half between the quartiles. os_moments() checks that the log-tails and the log-density are finite at a few points around the requested ranks. Neither check certifies accuracy. A distribution whose support has a finite end gives its endpoints in support.
  2. The tail indices decide which moments exist. Suppose the density decays like |x|−νL−1|x|^{-\nu_L - 1} in the lower tail and like x−νU−1x^{-\nu_U - 1} in the upper tail. Then the order statistic X(r)X_{(r)} has a finite second moment if and only if νLr>2\nu_L r > 2 and νU(n−r+1)>2\nu_U (n - r + 1) > 2. Declare (νL,νU)(\nu_L, \nu_U) in tail, with Inf for a tail that is bounded or decays faster than any power. A rank whose moment does not exist stops the computation, with an error that names the rank. The package cannot check the declared indices. The default tail = c(Inf, Inf) declares that every moment exists, so for a heavy-tailed distribution, omitting tail removes the check. A moment that does not exist then usually stops the computation with an integration error, but nothing guarantees it. So declare the tail indices of a heavy-tailed distribution. (For the built-in tt, Cauchy and FF families the package sets them.)
  3. Supply the distribution near the origin. The integrals are taken about the median of the supplied distribution, in units of its spread (Appendix A), so the scale on which it is supplied does not matter. The tests check that a normal supplied with a standard deviation from 0.001 to 10610^6 agrees with the scaled standard normal within 10−1110^{-11} in relative terms. Its position does matter. A distribution whose median is large against its spread, say 10810^8 with unit spread, makes x−Q(1/2)x - Q(1/2) a difference of two large numbers, which loses precision, and the computation stops with an error. Supply such a distribution near the origin and pass the shift as os_shift, which may be as large as needed: the tests compute the range of two uniform observations at os_shift = 1e16 exactly.
  4. Some distributions stop with an error rather than return a number. The integration range is cut around the peak of each order statistic and follows the tails of the distribution. The cut does not follow a second mode. For a mixture of two narrow normals, the mode that holds a tenth of the mass fell between the quadrature points. The package therefore integrates the density of every order statistic it computes by quadrature, and stops, naming the rank, when that mass is not 1. It also stops when a piece of the range cannot be resolved. This happens for a tail so heavy that the mass of the integrand lies far out, as for the covariances of a lognormal with sdlog = 3 or of a Weibull with shape 0.2, whose moments exist. It also happens for the covariance of an extreme order statistic whose variance barely exists, such as the minimum of 20 observations from a tt distribution with 2.05 to 2.3 degrees of freedom. For a user’s distribution whose density is infinite at an upper endpoint, the order statistics next to that endpoint are computed less accurately and are refused once they concentrate against it. Supplying the reflected variable, whose singular endpoint is the lower one at 0, brings that endpoint under the treatment of Appendix A. These checks catch some failures and certify none.
  5. Declare the points where the density is not smooth. The quadrature rule assumes an integrand that is smooth inside each piece of the integration range. A density with a kink or a jump inside its support, such as the Laplace density at its median or a triangular density at its mode, breaks that assumption. Give such points in the breaks argument of os_dist(), and the package cuts every integral there. For the Laplace distribution at n=5n = 5, the covariances sum to their exact value 10 within 10−1210^{-12} with breaks = 0, and within about 10−810^{-8} without it. The error estimate quad_err does not show that loss. A jump that is not declared usually stops the computation with an integration error. The package cannot find these points itself, and the built-in families have none. The help page of os_dist() has the Laplace example.

A Pareto distribution with shape 1.5 shows the second point. Its maximum has no variance, because νU(n−r+1)=1.5\nu_U (n - r + 1) = 1.5 at rank nn, which is not above 2, and the other ranks have one:

os_moments(5, ranks = 5, dist = pareto(1.5))
#> Error:
#> ! os_moments(): the moment of order 2 of X_(5) does not exist: the upper tail index 1.5 times n - r + 1 = 1 is not above 2
os_moments(5, ranks = 1:4, dist = pareto(1.5), cov = FALSE)$var
#>         r1         r2         r3         r4 
#> 0.03227542 0.12829478 0.51263572 3.91479400

Sample quantiles, linear combinations and the BLUE

This section shows the three functions that turn the moments of order statistics into the moments of the statistics computed from them. A sample quantile under any of the nine definitions of quantile() (Hyndman and Fan, 1996) is a fixed combination of two adjacent order statistics, so its moments follow from theirs. os_quantile_weights(p, n, type) gives the ranks and the weights, with R’s default type = 7 unless another of the nine definitions is named. os_lin_moments() turns them into moments. It returns the means in mean, the variances in var, and the covariance matrix of the statistics in cov. As a first case, take the median of an even-sized sample, which averages two order statistics. How does its variance compare with that of the median of the next odd size?

qw <- os_quantile_weights(p = 0.5, n = 10)   # type 7, R's default
qw$W   # one column per probability, rows named by rank
#>    50%
#> r5 0.5
#> r6 0.5
m10 <- os_moments(10, ranks = qw$ranks)
med10 <- os_lin_moments(qw$W, m10)
m11 <- os_moments(11, ranks = 6)
c(sd_median_n10 = sqrt(med10$var[[1]]), sd_median_n11 = sqrt(m11$var[[1]]))
#> sd_median_n10 sd_median_n11 
#>     0.3719226     0.3703545

For a standard normal sample of size 10, the median is the average of the fifth and sixth order statistics. The chunk prints its standard deviation next to that of the median of 11 observations, which is a single order statistic. The standard deviation of the median of ten is 1.0042 times that of the median of eleven.

os_lin_moments() takes any weights. With one column per statistic, it returns their means and their covariance matrix, so the range and the midrange of the same sample come together:

m <- os_moments(20, ranks = c(1, 20), dist = "logis")
W <- cbind(range = c(-1, 1), midrange = c(0.5, 0.5))
os_lin_moments(W, m)[c("mean", "cov")]
#> $mean
#>    range midrange 
#> 7.095479 0.000000 
#> 
#> $cov
#>             range  midrange
#> range    3.284619 0.0000000
#> midrange 0.000000 0.8750502

cov is the 2 by 2 covariance matrix of the range and the midrange. Their covariance is half the difference of the variances of the maximum and the minimum, which is zero for a symmetric parent such as the logistic.

The BLUE of location and scale of Lloyd (1952) use the moments of the available order statistics. Suppose a study reports only its five-number summary: the minimum, the three quartiles and the maximum of n=25n = 25 observations. If the data are normal, os_blue() gives the weights of the linear unbiased estimators of the mean and the standard deviation with the smallest variance, in w_mu and w_sigma. It also gives the variances of those estimators per unit of σ2\sigma^2, in var_mu and var_sigma. The chunk prints the weights and the standard errors in units of σ\sigma:

five <- c(1, 7, 13, 19, 25)   # the five-number ranks when n = 25 = 4 * 6 + 1
b <- os_blue(os_moments(25, ranks = five))
round(b$w_mu, 4)
#>     r1     r7    r13    r19    r25 
#> 0.0821 0.2857 0.2644 0.2857 0.0821
round(b$w_sigma, 4)
#>      r1      r7     r13     r19     r25 
#> -0.1713 -0.2566  0.0000  0.2566  0.1713
c(se_of_mean_estimate = sqrt(b$var_mu),
  se_of_sd_estimate = sqrt(b$var_sigma))
#> se_of_mean_estimate   se_of_sd_estimate 
#>           0.2068675           0.1585884

The standard error of the estimated mean is 0.2069 σ\sigma, against σ/25=0.2σ\sigma/\sqrt{25} = 0.2\,\sigma for the sample mean of all 25 observations. So the standard error from the five-number summary is 3.4% larger here. The scale that os_blue() estimates is the multiplier σ\sigma of the family’s standard member in μ+σZ\mu + \sigma Z: the standard deviation for the normal, the scale parameter for the logistic, the Gumbel, the gamma or the Weibull, and the length of the support for the uniform. The standard member ZZ carries the shape parameters of the call, such as the degrees of freedom of a tt distribution. The same call works for any family and any subset of two or more ranks whose covariance matrix is invertible. For example, here is the BLUE of a logistic location and scale from a complete sample of nine:

bl <- os_blue(os_moments(9, dist = "logis"))
round(bl$w_mu, 4)
#>     r1     r2     r3     r4     r5     r6     r7     r8     r9 
#> 0.0320 0.0901 0.1335 0.1600 0.1689 0.1600 0.1335 0.0901 0.0320
round(c(var_mu = bl$var_mu, var_sigma = bl$var_sigma,
        cov = bl$cov), 5)
#>    var_mu var_sigma       cov 
#>   0.34247   0.08627   0.00000

The covariance of the two estimators prints as zero, because the standard logistic is symmetric about zero and the rank set is complete. So the location and scale estimators are uncorrelated.

Appendix A: how the integrals are evaluated

This appendix states the integrals and the numerical design that evaluates them, for the reader who wants to know what “exact” rests on. The density of X(r)X_{(r)} and the joint density of X(r)X_{(r)} and X(s)X_{(s)}, r<sr < s, are fr:n(x)=n!(r−1)!(n−r)!F(x)r−1{1−F(x)}n−rf(x),fr,s:n(y,z)=n!(r−1)!(s−r−1)!(n−s)!F(y)r−1{F(z)−F(y)}s−r−1{1−F(z)}n−sf(y)f(z) \begin{aligned} f_{r:n}(x) &= \frac{n!}{(r-1)!\,(n-r)!} F(x)^{r-1} \{1 - F(x)\}^{n-r} f(x), \\ f_{r,s:n}(y, z) &= \frac{n!}{(r-1)!\,(s-r-1)!\,(n-s)!} F(y)^{r-1} \{F(z) - F(y)\}^{s-r-1} \{1 - F(z)\}^{n-s} f(y) f(z) \end{aligned} for y<zy < z, and the moments are their integrals against xx, x2x^2 and yzyz (David and Nagaraja, 2003). The package evaluates them with R’s integrate(), an adaptive rule that estimates its own error from the points where it evaluates the integrand. R’s help page warns that such a rule can miss a narrow peak that falls between its points and still report a small error. The design below is built around that warning and around the limits of double-precision floating-point numbers (“doubles” below). It has three parts: what is computed, how it is integrated, and how the integrand is evaluated. Wu and Tong (2026) give the reasons and the evidence in full.

What is computed. Two choices keep the quantities well scaled.

  • Standardized units. The integrals are taken in t={x−Q(1/2)}/σ̃t = \{x - Q(1/2)\}/\tilde\sigma, where QQ is the quantile function of the standard member and the spread σ̃\tilde\sigma is its interquartile range divided by that of the standard normal. So σ̃=1\tilde\sigma = 1 for the normal. The cut points and the integrator’s absolute tolerances below are then in the distribution’s own units, and a distribution supplied on any scale is computed as accurately as on scale one.
  • Each moment about the center of its own order statistic. The moments of X(r)X_{(r)} are taken about crc_r, the point Q(r/(n+1))Q(r/(n+1)) in these units. Without this centering, the variance of an order statistic far from the median would be the small difference of two moments of size cr2c_r^2, and it would lose its precision at large nn. Taken about crc_r, the variances of the uniform and the exponential order statistics we tested keep about ten significant digits up to n=106n = 10^6, and every correlation is reproduced within about 10−1010^{-10} in absolute terms. The one quantity that keeps fewer digits is the covariance of two nearly independent order statistics, such as the two extremes, whose correlation is of order 1/n1/n. Its relative error is the error of its correlation divided by the correlation, up to the relative errors of the two variances. The help page of os_moments() states the measured cases. The family’s other parameters, os_shift and os_multiplier are applied after the integration.

How it is integrated. Three rules keep the adaptive rule on the mass of each integrand.

  • A cut around the peak. The density of X(r)X_{(r)} concentrates near crc_r, in a region whose width shrinks like n−1/2n^{-1/2}. An adaptive rule started on the whole line can miss that region, and return a value near zero with a small claimed error. The package therefore cuts the range at cr±hrc_r \pm h_r, where hrh_r is ten large-sample standard deviations of the order statistic, drd_r, plus a minimum half-width of 4/n+14/\sqrt{n+1}. The peak then sits inside a finite piece. The first moment, whose integrand changes sign at crc_r, is cut there as well. The inner integral of a covariance is cut the same way, around the peak of X(s)X_{(s)}. Its outer integral is cut at the points of both order statistics, because the inner quadrature changes its pieces where the outer variable crosses them.
  • Tolerances scaled to the order statistic. The single integrals and the inner integrals run at a relative tolerance of 10−1110^{-11}, and the outer integrals at 10−910^{-9}. The inner tolerance is a hundred times tighter, so that the noise of the inner quadrature stays below what the outer rule resolves. The absolute tolerances are multiplied by min⁡(1,dr)\min(1, d_r) once for each factor of the moment: once for a first moment and twice for a second moment of X(r)X_{(r)}, by the factor of rank ss for the inner integral of a covariance, and by the factors of both ranks for its outer integral. The reason is that a narrow order statistic has small moments: the variance of the minimum of a million uniform observations is 7×10−127 \times 10^{-12} in standardized units, below a fixed tolerance that suits the normal. The inner integral’s absolute tolerance is also divided by max⁡(1,|y−cr|)\max(1, |y - c_r|), the outer factor that multiplies it, so that the far tail of a heavy-tailed distribution is not lost. With this, a lognormal with sdlog = 2 is accurate to about 10−910^{-9} in relative terms, rather than 10−1110^{-11}.
  • Refusal rules. integrate() may report a roundoff or subdivision problem on a piece of the range. The package accepts such a piece when its error estimate is below 10−1010^{-10}, multiplied by the same factors as the tolerances. Otherwise it stops the computation with an error. A piece on an infinite range that integrate() reports as probably divergent is accepted only when its value is below that scaled 10−1010^{-10} as well. The density of every order statistic is also integrated and must have mass 1 within 10−710^{-7}, and a variance that comes out zero or negative stops the computation.

A density that is infinite at a finite endpoint of the support needs one more rule. A gamma, a chi-square, a Weibull, a beta or an FF distribution with a shape aa below 1 has a density that grows like ea−1e^{a-1} in the distance ee from the endpoint, and an extreme order statistic can sit so close to the endpoint that the centered variable tt cannot tell its points apart. Next to such an endpoint the package integrates in v=eav = e^a. In this variable the distribution function is nearly linear, the integrand is bounded, and the distance from the endpoint is the integration variable itself, so an order statistic far closer to the endpoint than tt resolves is still placed. For a built-in family aa is the family’s own shape, and for a user’s distribution with an infinite density at a lower endpoint the package estimates it from the distribution function. The upper endpoint of the built-in beta is treated through 1−X1 - X, which is the beta with its two shapes exchanged. The range is also cut around the peak of the order statistic in the variable vv, because that peak is far narrower than the pieces of the ordinary cut. The tests assert the result against exact values: the minimum of 1001 Weibull observations with shape 0.3, and the minimum of a million observations from a beta(aa, 1) at a=0.5a = 0.5, 0.1 and 0.05, agree with their closed forms within 10−1010^{-10} for the mean and 10−910^{-9} for the variance in relative terms.

How the integrand is evaluated. Two rules keep each value of the integrand accurate.

  • The logarithmic scale. The factorials overflow doubles (n!n! alone does from n=171n = 171 on), and the powers of the tail probabilities underflow to zero at large nn. So the package works with logarithms. The log of the coefficient comes from lbeta(), the log powers of the tails from p(x, log.p = TRUE) and p(x, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE), and the log density from d(x, log = TRUE). The sum is exponentiated once. Working on the log scale is the approach of Royston (1982) for the means of normal order statistics, carried to the product moments.
  • No cancellation in F(z)−F(y)F(z) - F(y). When both points lie above the median, F(y)F(y) and F(z)F(z) are close to one, and their difference loses its relative precision. The package therefore forms the difference on the side where the probabilities are small. It computes F(z){1−F(y)/F(z)}F(z)\{1 - F(y)/F(z)\} when both points lie below the median, and S(y){1−S(z)/S(y)}S(y)\{1 - S(z)/S(y)\} with S=1−FS = 1 - F when both lie above it. The logarithm of the difference then keeps its relative precision.

The closed forms used by default are the beta and Dirichlet moments of the uniform, the exponential’s representation as a sum of independent exponential spacings, the digamma and trigamma forms of the logistic means and variances, and the Gumbel maximum, whose law is a shifted Gumbel.

Appendix B: the checks behind the numbers

This appendix lists the checks that run inside the package and the checks that its tests assert. Their purpose is that a quadrature failure shows up as a residual or a failed test, rather than as a wrong number. A variance that comes out zero or negative always stops the computation with an error. When check = TRUE, the default, two checks run if their conditions are met, and their residuals are stored in checks. A residual above 10−610^{-6} raises a warning, and so does a covariance matrix with a negative eigenvalue beyond rounding. These checks catch some failures of the quadrature and certify none, because a failure that every integral shares can satisfy them.

  • Reflection symmetry, for a symmetric distribution and a set of ranks that is closed under r↦n+1−rr \mapsto n + 1 - r. The means are antisymmetric and the second moments symmetric about the median. The integrators do not impose this, so a violation signals a quadrature failure. For such rank sets, the covariances are computed for half of the pairs and reflected.
  • The permutation identities, when every rank is requested. The order statistics are then a permutation of the sample, so ∑rαr=nE[X]\sum_r \alpha_r = n E[X], ∑rE[X(r)2]=nE[X2]\sum_r E[X^2_{(r)}] = n E[X^2] and ∑r,sBrs=nVar(X)\sum_{r,s} B_{rs} = n\,\mathrm{Var}(X), for any parent with a finite second moment. For the normal, every row of BB also sums to σ2\sigma^2, because the sample mean is independent of every deviation from it. That row identity does not hold for other parents in general. The exponential at n=2n = 2 has row sums 1/21/2 and 3/23/2. A symmetric parent has unit row sums at n=2n = 2 by symmetry, but the uniform fails at n=3n = 3.

The package’s tests assert the following when R CMD check runs them. The comparison with the earlier implementation, the second-last item, is skipped on CRAN to save time.

  • the uniform and exponential closed forms at the five ranks of a five-number summary and at all their pairs, for n=20n = 20, 100100 and 10011001, within 10−1010^{-10}.
  • the logistic means and variances and the Gumbel maximum within 10−1010^{-10}, and the n=2n = 2 covariances of the logistic and the Gumbel, which follow from X(1)X(2)=X1X2X_{(1)} X_{(2)} = X_1 X_2.
  • the variance of the Cauchy median of five against the integral on the uniform scale, within 10−910^{-9}.
  • the permutation identities for the first five families by quadrature at n=5n = 5, 99 and 1313, within 10−910^{-9}, and the unit row sums for the normal.
  • for the eight families added in version 0.3.0: the Weibull against its closed-form moments at shapes 0.3, 0.5 and 2, at the two lowest ranks for n=5n = 5 and 101 and at the minimum of 1001 for shape 0.3, within 10−1010^{-10} for the means and 10−910^{-9} for the variances in relative terms; the minimum of 101, 1001 and 3001 observations from a beta(0.1, 1) and of a million observations from a beta(aa, 1) at a=0.5a = 0.5, 0.1 and 0.05, the maximum of the reflected distribution, and the covariances next to the endpoint, against their exact values; the tt with 2 degrees of freedom against its closed-form moments; the permutation identities against the exact moments of the parent at n=8n = 8 for the tt, gamma, chi-square, beta, lognormal, Weibull and FF families, including shapes below 1; the special cases that coincide with a family that has closed forms (a gamma or a Weibull with shape 1, a beta with both shapes 1); and the refusal of each moment that does not exist for the tt, the Cauchy and the FF.
  • that the split of a family’s parameters into the standard member, a shift and a multiplier returns the scaled moments of the standard member.
  • the tables of Tietjen, Kahaner and Beckman (1976) at the five-number ranks for n=5n = 5 to 4949, which is 240 printed entries. One of them is illegible in the available scan and is skipped. The package agrees with 206 of the others within the table’s certified accuracy of 10−710^{-7}. It differs by more than 10−710^{-7} from 33 quartile entries at n=29n = 29 to 4949, by up to 1.4×10−41.4 \times 10^{-4}. We evaluated those 33 entries once more in the probability scale, through the beta density of the uniform order statistic, which shares nothing with the package’s integrand. That evaluation agrees with the package within 4×10−164 \times 10^{-16}, so we take the 33 entries to be errors of the printed table.
  • Harter’s (1960) mean and variance of the normal range at 24 sample sizes from 5 to 97, within 2×10−82 \times 10^{-8}.
  • a gamma distribution with shape 2, supplied through os_dist(), against its exact means and variances at every rank for n=5n = 5 and 1010, which are finite sums of rationals, within 10−1010^{-10}.
  • the quadrature against the uniform and exponential closed forms at the minimum, the lower quartile, the median and the maximum for n=104n = 10^4, 10510^5 and 10610^6. The variances and the covariances of neighboring ranks agree within 10−910^{-9} in relative terms. The covariance of the two extremes agrees within 10−910^{-9} at n=104n = 10^4 and within 10−310^{-3} at n=105n = 10^5 and 10610^6.
  • a normal supplied with standard deviations from 10−310^{-3} to 10610^6 against the standard normal’s moments scaled, within 10−1110^{-11} in relative terms.
  • the minimum of 10, 100, 1000 and 10510^5 observations from a beta(1/2, 1/2) supplied through os_dist() against a quadrature in the probability scale, within 10−1010^{-10} in relative terms for the mean, and the maximum of a thousand and of 10510^5, next to the upper endpoint, refused with an error. For the built-in beta the two extremes of 1001 observations are computed and mirror each other.
  • the covariance of the two order statistics of two beta(1/2, 1/2) observations against its exact value 4/π44/\pi^4, within 10−910^{-9}.
  • a mixture of two narrow normals refused by the mass check, and the range of two uniform observations at os_shift = 1e16 computed exactly.
  • the covariance of the two order statistics of two lognormal observations with sdlog = 2 against its exact value, within 2×10−72 \times 10^{-7} on a value of 38.8.
  • the normal at the five-number ranks against an earlier implementation of the same method for the normal, written separately before the package, at 39 sample sizes from 5 to 1001, within 10−1010^{-10}.
  • the quantile weights against quantile() for all nine types, and the BLUE against its generalized least squares definition.
